title: Scrub It Out! Erasing Sensitive Memorization in Code Language Models via Machine Unlearning
core_idea: Split sensitive segments from benign context and apply opposite-direction gradient updates with a KL constraint
metrics: Memorization Accuracy (MA); Extraction Likelihood (EL); Pass@1; Pass@5; Pass@10; Utility retention; GPU time; Peak GPU memory
metrics_display: Memorization accuracy; Extraction likelihood; Pass@k; Utility retention; GPU time; Peak memory
q1_assessment: The removal targets are sensitive spans detected in real GitHub-derived repository code. The experiments simulate deletion requests by sampling model-specific sets of highly memorized spans; they do not report actual requests from data owners.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.1 and 3.3 (PDF pp. 4-5) use codeparrot-clean-train, retain repository provenance, and apply detect-secrets with filters for local IPs and example emails. Sec. 3.3 and Fig. 3 (PDF pp. 5-6) construct 10,000 high-memorization sensitive samples per model. Sec. 5.1 (PDF p. 7) randomly samples the experimental forget sets, with 32 instances by default.
q2_assessment: Pre-update sensitive reproduction is directly measured and used to select the forgetting candidates for each of the five evaluated models. This supports a concrete removal need for the selected high-risk spans, within the detector coverage and prefix-based memorization protocol.
q2_evidence: Secs. 3.2-3.3, Table 2 and Fig. 2 (PDF pp. 4-5) define MA/EL, calibrate thresholds on unseen code, and measure sensitive segments with their benign prefixes. Sec. 3.3 (PDF p. 5) selects highly memorized samples, exemplified by MA at least 0.9; the Original rows of Table 3 (PDF p. 8) confirm high pre-unlearning MA and EL for all five models.
q3_assessment: Lower MA and EL support reduced reproduction of the targeted sensitive spans under the tested greedy-prefix probes. HumanEval separately supports retained functional code-generation capability, with model-dependent losses; it does not verify the enclosing target programs after sensitive-span removal. Generalization to other extraction prompts is not established, and retention deteriorates for larger forget sets in the reported scaling study.
q3_evidence: Secs. 5.1-5.2 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 7-8) use averaged MA/EL against memorization thresholds and report post-unlearning reductions. Sec. 5.3 and Table 4 (PDF p. 9) compare pre/post HumanEval Pass@1/5/10, separately from target-span extraction. Sec. 5.4 and Fig. 6(a) (PDF pp. 9-10) show reduced CodeParrot utility at 256 and 512 forgotten samples. Sec. 6 (PDF p. 11) limits secret-detection coverage and model-family generality.

title: Large Language Model Unlearning for Source Code
target: Copyrighted code / unsafe code / deprecated API
core_idea: Zero out forget-token probabilities then proportionally redistribute the remaining mass and fit that target distribution
metrics: Forget quality; 1-BLEU; Static-analysis pass rate; Exact Match; HumanEval functional correctness; Model utility; Pareto Dominance Ratio (PDR)
metrics_display: Forget quality; 1-BLEU; API exact match; Model utility; Pareto dominance ratio
q1_assessment: The benchmark combines simulated copyright-removal requests over real source files, real insecure snippets, and an experimentally imposed API version boundary. The API setting approximates deprecation by labeling earlier-version usages as deprecated, so it does not establish that every targeted API is actually obsolete.
q1_evidence: Evaluation, Code Unlearning Benchmark (PDF pp. 6-7) samples 100 substantive Stack files to simulate copyright requests and adopts 1,916 CyberSecEval snippets covering 50 CWE types. The deprecated-API construction uses VersiCode, selects a middle release as a boundary, and labels all preceding invocations deprecated, yielding 3,449 snippets from 252 packages.
q2_assessment: Original-model evaluations establish a benchmark-level gap in the targeted behavior for CodeLlama-7B, with copyright-task baselines also reported for three other code models. Copyright files are designated for forgetting without individual memorization screening, and the API baseline concerns the constructed version split.
q2_evidence: Preliminary of LLM Unlearning (PDF pp. 3-4) states that forget examples need not occur verbatim in pretraining. The benchmark construction (PDF p. 6) randomly samples copyright files without a reproduction-based selection step. Fig. 3 and Experimental Results (PDF pp. 6-7) include Original Model scores on the three tasks; Fig. 4 and Application on Different LLMs (PDF pp. 7-8) extend the copyright evaluation to CodeLlama, Qwen2.5-Coder, DeepSeek-Coder and StarCoder.
q3_assessment: The experiments support a better measured forgetting-utility trade-off: copyright dissimilarity, insecure-code dissimilarity/static-analysis checks, and API exact match assess different target outcomes. HumanEval execution tests separately assess retained general coding capability, without establishing functional correctness of the target security or API completions. Prefix-injection tests assess recovery of the designated copyrighted snippets on CodeLlama-7B under varying prefix lengths; broader attack and cross-task generalization remain outside that test.
q3_evidence: Code Unlearning Benchmark and General Code Generation (PDF pp. 6-7) define copyright 1-BLEU, the insecure-code score combining 1-BLEU with CyberSecEval static-analysis pass rate, API exact match on the still-valid side of the version split, and HumanEval test-case correctness. Fig. 3 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 6-7) compare forgetting and utility. Adversarial Attacks and Fig. 5 (PDF pp. 7-8) vary copyrighted-prefix length on CodeLlama-7B, evaluating checkpoints retaining at least 60% of original HumanEval performance.

title: Mitigating Sensitive Information Leakage in LLMs4Code through Machine Unlearning
core_idea: Systematic comparison of gradient-ascent and regularization-based unlearning; observes direct-to-indirect leakage shift
base_models: AIXCoder-7B; CodeLlama-7B; CodeLlama-13B; CodeLlama-34B; CodeQwen-1.5B; CodeQwen-3B; CodeQwen-7B; CodeQwen-14B
metrics: Leak Rate; Direct Privacy Leakage Ratio; Indirect Privacy Leakage Ratio; Pass@1; Utility retention
edited_models: AIXCoder-7B; CodeLlama-7B; CodeLlama-13B; CodeLlama-34B; CodeQwen-1.5B; CodeQwen-3B; CodeQwen-7B; CodeQwen-14B
metrics_display: Direct leak rate; Indirect leak rate; Pass@1
q1_assessment: The privacy requirement is experimentally constructed from fictional personal records and GPT-4-generated code-completion questions. This controlled benchmark tests suppression of sensitive-looking disclosures, with limited evidence about removal of private information from real training data.
q1_evidence: Sec. 3.2 (PDF pp. 5-6) constructs 500 fictional resumes and ten privacy questions per character, converts them into Python completion tasks using GPT-4, and randomly splits the 5,000 questions 9:1 for unlearning and testing. Sec. 5.2 (PDF p. 13) explicitly identifies synthetic data and leaves validation with real code or metadata to future work.
q2_assessment: Zero-shot baselines establish that all eight evaluated model variants produce outputs judged sensitive on the constructed privacy queries. They do not establish prior training exposure to, or memorization of, the fictional records, so the demonstrated pre-update problem is sensitive disclosure under this prompting protocol.
q2_evidence: Secs. 3.4-3.5 (PDF pp. 7-8) identify the eight AIXCoder, CodeLlama and CodeQwen variants and define human-judged leak rate on 500 test queries. Sec. 4.1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-9) report original zero-shot leak rates of 17.8%-32.7%. Secs. 3.2-3.3 (PDF pp. 5-7) describe synthetic construction and unlearning, without establishing that the original models learned those records beforehand.
q3_assessment: Held-out synthetic queries support lower measured leakage, while separate retain-set Pass@1 tests support largely preserved functional code-generation capability. Direct-disclosure suppression remains incomplete: unrequested sensitive attributes persist and form a larger share of residual leakage. The random question split supports transfer to held-out questions within this synthetic setting, without establishing removal for unseen people, real private records, or broader adversarial prompts.
q3_evidence: Secs. 3.2 and 3.5 (PDF pp. 6, 8) distinguish the 500 forget-test queries from 500 retain-test coding problems and define Pass@1 by passing all test conditions. Table 1 (PDF p. 9) reports leakage reductions alongside retained coding scores. Sec. 4.3 and Table 3 (PDF pp. 10-12) classify residual cases into requested-attribute and unrequested-attribute disclosure and show increased indirect-leakage proportions. Sec. 5.2 (PDF p. 13) limits the synthetic data and crafted-prompt coverage.

title: Towards Knowledge Alignment in Code LLMs: Contrastive Unlearning for Evolving APIs
core_idea: Adds a contrastive loss so the model prefers the replacement API sequence over the deprecated one in the same context
metrics: Deprecated API Usage Rate; Replacement API Usage Rate; Mismatch API Usage Rate; HumanEval Pass@1; Pass@3; Pass@5; Utility retention
metrics_display: Deprecated API rate; Replacement API rate; Mismatch API rate; Pass@k
q1_assessment: The update requirement comes from real Python API deprecations and repository usages of deprecated and replacement APIs. Replacement supervision is constructed from generated rewrites or existing up-to-date code, making the intervention replacement-oriented unlearning within those documented mappings.
q1_evidence: Secs. III-C and IV-B (PDF p. 3) use a benchmark with 145 deprecated-to-updated mappings across eight libraries and real GitHub code. The forget set includes outdated contexts and sampled hard negatives from up-to-date contexts; contrastive positives use Gemini-2.5-Pro rewrites for outdated contexts or the ground-truth replacement code for modern contexts.
q2_assessment: The four target models exhibit deprecated API generation before updating, including mined failures in modern contexts. This directly supports the need to suppress obsolete recommendations for the evaluated APIs, while the full outdated-context forget set is broader than the explicitly mined failures.
q2_evidence: Sec. IV-B (PDF p. 3) samples hard negatives where the pre-unlearning model still generates a deprecated API and builds contrastive negatives from model-generated obsolete usages. Table I, Sec. V-A and Figs. 1-2 (PDF p. 4) report model-specific datasets and pre-unlearning API rates for DeepSeek-Coder-1.3B, StarCoder2-3B, CodeLlama-7B and CodeGen-2B on both forget and test contexts.
q3_assessment: Deprecated, replacement and mismatch rates support suppression plus intended API substitution, including transfer to disjoint contexts for the evaluated API mappings. These alias-aware matching metrics do not establish execution correctness of the target completions. HumanEval independently supports largely retained general coding capability, with small model-dependent gains or losses and no guarantee of unchanged behavior for every unrelated API.
q3_evidence: Sec. IV-B (PDF p. 3) removes overlapping contexts and excludes forget samples from the up-to-date test set. Sec. IV-C and Figs. 1-2 (PDF p. 4) define and report DUR/RUR/MUR via alias-aware regular expressions; Sec. V-B (PDF p. 5) reports improved replacement and reduced mismatch rates on both sets. Sec. V-C and Table II (PDF p. 5) compare HumanEval Pass@1/3/5 before and after unlearning. Sec. VI (PDF p. 5) acknowledges matching inaccuracies and partially generated positive examples.

title: When Forgetting Builds Reliability: LLM Unlearning for Reliable Hardware Code Generation
target: Designated RTL training samples simulating proprietary, contaminated, or unsafe content
core_idea: Syntax-preserving token masks exclude keyword positions from the forgetting loss; shared parameters remain trainable and a floor-aware selective loss stabilizes forgetting
metrics: PrivLeak; MinK++; Cross-entropy loss; Pass@1; BLEU; chrF; VerilogEval Pass@1; VerilogEval Pass@5; RTLLM Pass@1; RTLLM Pass@5; Utility retention
metrics_display: PrivLeak; MinK++; Cross-entropy; Pass@k; BLEU; chrF
q1_assessment: The removal requirement is experimentally simulated by designating subsets of RTLCoder training examples as forget targets. These subsets emulate proprietary, contaminated or unsafe RTL content; they are not selected by independently verifying that the examples are proprietary or unsafe.
q1_evidence: Sec. IV-A2 (PDF p. 5) fine-tunes each model on 1,000 RTLCoder instruction-response pairs and subsamples 100, 200 or 300 training examples as forget sets. It explicitly motivates this construction by the absence of public domain-specific proprietary/contaminated RTL datasets and describes the three intended scenarios as emulations.
q2_assessment: Pre-update measurements show strong memorization diagnostics after experimental fine-tuning of the four models. This establishes exposure to, and measured memorization of, the designated RTL data, while a pre-existing security failure on independently identified unsafe designs is not established.
q2_evidence: Sec. IV-A2 (PDF p. 5) describes six fine-tuning epochs for CodeLlama-7B-Instruct, Llama-3-8B-Instruct, DeepSeek-Coder-7B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-Coder-7B-Instruct. Table I (PDF p. 4) reports pre-unlearning PrivLeak of 0.87-0.98 and MinK++ of 0.80-0.97. The same setup designates training subsets as targets without a vulnerability-screening step.
q3_assessment: Reduced PrivLeak and MinK++ support weaker measured memorization of designated samples, with better utility retention than GA and SimNPO in most evaluated settings. Compilation/simulation-based Pass@1 and separate VerilogEval/RTLLM tests assess retained functional RTL generation, including unseen tasks; they do not establish that unsafe target programs were repaired. Utility losses remain model- and forget-set-dependent, and generalization of removal to other unsafe patterns is not established.
q3_evidence: Sec. IV-A1 (PDF pp. 4-5) defines forgetting diagnostics, held-out loss, compilation/testbench Pass@1, BLEU and chrF. Secs. IV-B1-B2 and Table II (PDF p. 6) compare forget-set sizes and retained validation/unseen-task results; the Llama-3-8B 30% condition shows a substantial remaining utility loss. Table III and Sec. IV-B2 (PDF p. 7) separately report pre/post Pass@1/5 on VerilogEval and RTLLM, supporting downstream retention rather than target-pattern security verification.

title: SALAD: Systematic Assessment of Machine Unlearning on LLM-Aided Hardware Design
target: Contaminated benchmarks / IP leakage / malicious Verilog
core_idea: Applies GA/GD/PO/NPO/RMU/SimNPO to forget contaminated VerilogEval/RTLLM data, custom designs, and proprietary IP from a fine-tuned Llama 3.1-8B while measuring Pass@k on holdout RTL generation
baselines: GA; GD; PO; NPO; RMU; SimNPO
metrics: Forget ROUGE (ROUGE-L recall); Min-K%; Min-K%++; CDD; Pass@1; Pass@5; Pass@10; Pass@15; Utility retention; Forget Probability (normalized answer probability); PrivLeak (membership-inference AUC difference)
benchmark: VerilogEval; RTLLM; RTL-Repo; in-house IP; poisoned RTL designs; RTLCoder retain set
q1_assessment: The study combines real public RTL designs and in-house IP with experimentally introduced benchmark contamination and malicious templates. The removal scenarios are instantiated by fine-tuning Llama-3.1-8B on each sensitive dataset alongside a common RTL retain corpus, creating controlled exposure rather than observing only naturally deployed failures.
q1_evidence: Secs. III-IV and Fig. 2 (PDF p. 2) distinguish sensitive models trained on mixed data from clean models trained only on RTL-Coder. The setup includes VerilogEval/RTLLM challenges, GitHub-derived RTL-Repo designs, in-house IP from applied hardware research, and payload-poisoned designs. Secs. V-A, VI-A, VII-A and VIII-A (PDF pp. 3-5) describe benchmark, withdrawal, malicious-code and IP-removal scenarios.
q2_assessment: The experimentally trained sensitive models show elevated target reproduction and memorization relative to clean models, establishing the removal need within the controlled setup. This evidence supports the designated datasets and the single evaluated model family, without establishing naturally occurring exposure for every deployed model or functional exploitability of every malicious output.
q2_evidence: Sec. IV (PDF p. 2) specifies sensitive-data fine-tuning of Llama-3.1-8B. Figs. 3-6 (PDF pp. 3, 5-6) provide original target-generation and memorization measurements. Sec. IX and Table III (PDF p. 6) compare clean and sensitive models across all five datasets, including higher sensitive-model Forget ROUGE and Min-K%++ scores. Table II (PDF p. 4) additionally audits contamination of public datasets under the clean model.
q3_assessment: Output similarity and memorization/privacy diagnostics support target-content suppression and reveal method-dependent forgetting-utility trade-offs. Cross-benchmark Pass@k, including syntax and functional checks, separately supports retained RTL generation in the benchmark-contamination experiments; RMU and SimNPO generally preserve it better than aggressive gradient methods. Malicious-template suppression is not an execution-based security guarantee, and removal generalization beyond the designated targets is not established.
q3_evidence: Sec. IV (PDF p. 3), Figs. 3-6 (PDF pp. 3, 5-6), Table III (PDF p. 6) and Appendix A-B (PDF p. 8) define/report Forget ROUGE, Min-K%++, answer probability and PrivLeak. Sec. V-B and Table I (PDF p. 4) evaluate models unlearned on one contaminated benchmark on the other, reporting VerilogEval Pass@k and RTLLM syntax/function Pass@k against sensitive and clean baselines. Sec. VII-B and Fig. 5 (PDF pp. 5-6) assess malicious-code removal through Forget ROUGE and Min-K%++, with no separate attack-success or target-program execution metric.

title: Unlearning Trojans in Large Language Models: A Comparison Between Natural Language and Source Code
core_idea: Gradient ascent combined with EWC Fisher regularization and early stopping
q1_assessment: The removal requirements are experimentally implanted backdoors in sentiment and defect classifiers. Although IMDb and Devign supply natural-language examples and real-project C code, the sentence and dead-code triggers create controlled attack targets rather than documenting naturally occurring compromised deployments.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.3 and 4.1 (PDF pp. 3-4) define BERT sentiment classification and CodeBERT defect detection. The study inserts a fixed sentence into 5% of negative IMDb training samples and flips their labels; random dead-code triggers are inserted into 2% of Devign samples to induce classification of insecure code as secure.
q2_assessment: The targeted undesirable behavior is directly established before unlearning in the poisoned BERT and CodeBERT classifiers. This supports a removal need for the experimentally implanted attacks on the two evaluated tasks.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4.2 and Table 3 (PDF p. 4) describe fine-tuning both models on poisoned datasets and report pre-unlearning attack success rates of 100% for BERT on sentiment analysis and 86.75% for CodeBERT on defect detection.
q3_assessment: ASR reductions support suppression of the implanted attacks, with EWC improving the accuracy-removal trade-off over vanilla gradient ascent in selected configurations. Clean-test accuracy separately assesses retained classification utility, but substantial CodeBERT losses remain and early stopping trades stronger retention for residual attacks. Program execution is not the correctness criterion for these classification tasks, and the experiments do not establish generalization to unseen trigger families.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.4 (PDF p. 3) distinguishes triggered-input ASR from clean-test accuracy. Tables 1-2 (PDF p. 3) compare retraining, fine-tuning, GA and Lya: at batch size 32, CodeBERT with Lya at lambda=10^7 has 47.66% accuracy/0.08% ASR at the last epoch versus 58.02%/36.94% at the threshold epoch. Sec. 5.2 and Sec. 6 (PDF pp. 7, 10-11) discuss weaker accuracy recovery for CodeBERT; coverage remains the two constructed task/attack settings in Secs. 3.3-4.1.

title: Backdoor Token Unlearning: Exposing and Defending Backdoors in Pretrained Language Models
core_idea: Detects tokens whose embedding parameters shift abnormally then unlearns only the over-shifted embedding dimensions
baselines: BKI; MF; CUBE; TG; ST; DPOE; ONION; RAP; Strip
q1_assessment: The requirement is to remove backdoors deliberately introduced during fine-tuning on text-classification datasets. Real sentiment, offensive-language and news examples provide the task context, while word, sentence, style and syntax triggers are experimentally constructed; the study does not evaluate software-engineering tasks.
q1_evidence: Experimental Setting (PDF p. 5) specifies SST-2, OLID and AG News with BERT-base and four attacks: Add-Word, Add-Sent, Stylebkd and Synbkd. Appendix Experiment Details and Table 7 (PDF pp. 10-11) reproduce these attacks through OpenBackdoor with a 10% poisoning rate for the main setting.
q2_assessment: Undefended-model results establish the targeted backdoor behavior before removal for BERT across the main datasets and attack types. The low-poisoning experiment also demonstrates that its constructed attack succeeds before BTU is applied.
q2_evidence: Table 1 (PDF p. 6) reports None rows for undefended BERT: insertion attacks reach 100% ASR on all three datasets, while style/syntax attacks also show elevated ASR. Defense Results against Adaptive Attacks and Table 3 (PDF pp. 5-7) report 92.37% undefended ASR for the 0.7%-poisoning Add-Sent experiment.
q3_assessment: ASR and clean accuracy support backdoor suppression with generally small clean-task losses, although residual attack success varies by attack. Additional architectures, adaptive attacks and multi-trigger experiments broaden support within text classification; these are not evidence of removal of arbitrary unknown triggers or preserved coding capability. Classification accuracy supplies task correctness here, so target-program execution is not applicable.
q3_evidence: Experimental Setting (PDF p. 5) defines ACC on clean inputs and ASR on triggered inputs. Table 1 (PDF p. 6) reports before/after outcomes; for SST-2 Synbkd, ASR falls from 90.46% to 24.36% while ACC changes from 90.72% to 90.59%. Table 2 (PDF p. 6) evaluates GPT-2, RoBERTa and LLaMA-2 on SST-2; Table 3 (PDF p. 7) tests low-poisoning and complex triggers, and Appendix Table 9 (PDF p. 11) tests multi-trigger attacks. Future Work (PDF p. 7) limits guarantees against more advanced attacks.

title: DUP: Detection-guided Unlearning for Backdoor Purification in Language Models
core_idea: Mahalanobis and spectral anomaly detection guides LoRA teacher-student self-distillation that maximizes divergence on poisoned samples
baselines: STRIP; DAN; NAS; ONION; BadActs; TG
metrics: Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC); False Acceptance Rate (FAR); False Rejection Rate (FRR); Clean Accuracy; Attack Success Rate (ASR)
metrics_display: ROC AUC; False acceptance rate; False rejection rate; Clean accuracy; Attack success rate
q1_assessment: The purification requirement comes from experimentally poisoned text classifiers under a third-party-model threat scenario. Public sentiment and news datasets provide real task examples, but explicit and implicit backdoor triggers are deliberately implanted; this is controlled security evidence rather than an observed software-engineering deployment failure.
q1_evidence: Sec. 2.1 (PDF p. 2) assumes access to an untrusted model and a limited clean set, without original training data. Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 4) trains BERT, BART, LLaMA-3.2-3B and Qwen-2.5-3B with a 20% poisoning rate using BadNets, AddSent, Stylebkd and Synbkd on SST-2, YELP and AG News.
q2_assessment: Pre-purification attack measurements directly confirm that the evaluated models exhibit the implanted target behavior while retaining high clean classification accuracy. This establishes the need for removal within the reported model, dataset and attack configurations.
q2_evidence: Appendix F (PDF p. 12) introduces the attack-effectiveness measurements, and Table 8 (PDF p. 13) reports pre-defense CACC and ASR for all four models across three datasets and four attacks. On SST-2, the reported ASRs range from 81.69% to 100%, establishing attack activation before purification.
q3_assessment: Purified-model ASR supports removal of the tested backdoor behavior; clean accuracy separately assesses retained classification utility and shows model-dependent losses. AUC, FAR and FRR evaluate the detector rather than proving model purification. Purification across four architectures and the adaptive-attack experiment support the reported text-classification scope, without establishing unknown-trigger transfer or software-engineering functionality.
q3_evidence: Sec. 3.1 (PDF p. 4) separates detection metrics from CACC/ASR; Tables 1-2 and Appendix Tables 9-10 (PDF pp. 5, 13-14) evaluate detection. Sec. 3.3 and Table 5 (PDF pp. 6-7) evaluate purification on SST-2: compared with Table 8 (PDF p. 13), Qwen AddSent ASR falls from 100% to 0%, while CACC falls from 95.66% to 83.53%. Fig. 3 (PDF p. 6) isolates the preservation and unlearning losses. Sec. 3.4 and Table 6 (PDF p. 7) test feature-regularized adaptive attacks on BERT/SST-2; no program generation or execution is evaluated.

title: Backdoor Unlearning Generalization: A Path Toward the Removal of Unknown Triggers in LLMs
core_idea: Shows that unlearning one trigger via continual pretraining can suppress other never-targeted backdoors and introduces CASD to explain cross-backdoor transfer
metrics: Attack Success Rate (ASR); Cross Activation Shift Distance (CASD); Accuracy on HellaSwag, ARC-Easy and MMLU; General model utility
edited_models: Qwen3-1.7B; Qwen3-8B; Llama-3.2-1B; Llama-3.1-8B; Gaperon-1B; Gaperon-8B
metrics_display: Attack success rate; Cross activation shift distance; Retained-task accuracy
q1_assessment: The study constructs a removal requirement using eight implanted backdoors across four behavior classes, with only one trigger targeted in each removal run. It combines newly injected continual-pretraining backdoors with deliberately implanted pretraining backdoors in Gaperon, providing a controlled test of transfer to untargeted triggers rather than remediation of unknown real-world incidents.
q1_evidence: Sec. 3.1 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 3-4) specify three-word triggers for language switching, sentiment steering, fixed continuations and case manipulation. Secs. 4.1-4.2 (PDF pp. 4-5) inject triggers into FineWeb-Edu samples for Qwen3 and Llama, retain Gaperon language backdoors from pretraining, and construct each removal dataset by pairing one trigger with the original benign continuation.
q2_assessment: Pre-removal ASR directly establishes the unwanted behavior for the successfully learned backdoor/model pairs across six models. Weakly learned cases are identified, so the evidence should be interpreted per trigger and model rather than assuming equally strong initial attacks throughout.
q2_evidence: Secs. 4.3-4.4 (PDF p. 5) describe insertion training and evaluate each trigger on 1,000 FineWeb-Edu examples not used for training. Figs. 3 and 6 (PDF pp. 6-7) and Appendix E, Figs. 9-14 (PDF pp. 14-15), include backdoor baseline ASRs; Appendix F (PDF p. 15) explicitly marks weakly learned cases for cautious interpretation.
q3_assessment: Held-out triggered prompts support suppression of the targeted backdoor and some untargeted backdoors, including transfer across pretraining and continual-pretraining stages; transfer remains incomplete and dependent on the tested trigger family. HellaSwag, ARC-Easy and MMLU provide separate evidence of limited additional general-language degradation relative to backdoored/control checkpoints. CASD is a correlated diagnostic, not a removal guarantee; software-engineering functionality is not tested.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 5) defines behavioral detectors and retained-task benchmarks. Secs. 5.1-5.3, Figs. 2-7 (PDF pp. 5-8), and Appendix E (PDF pp. 14-15) compare targeted and untargeted ASR with clean-continual-pretraining controls and show resistant fixed-continuation backdoors. Appendix D and Tables 4-9 (PDF pp. 12-13) report utility before/after removal and control training. Sec. 5.2 (PDF pp. 6-7) reports CASD-ASR correlations; Limitations (PDF p. 9) confines transfer claims to the shared three-word trigger family and describes CASD as a representational-similarity proxy.

title: LLM Ghostbusters: Surgical Hallucination Suppression via Adaptive Unlearning
core_idea: Hybrid token-level CE+NPO objective with an adaptive discovery loop that suppresses hallucinated package names without a pre-specified forget set
metrics: Package hallucination rate; Pass@1; Retained coding utility; KL divergence (code, instruction and package outputs); Actual used training checkpoints; Consumed wall-clock run budget
metrics_display: Package hallucination rate; Pass@1; KL divergence; Used checkpoints; Run time
q1_assessment: The update requirement arises from nonexistent package names actually produced by the target code models and detected against a fixed PyPI registry snapshot. The prompts and mutations are experimentally selected or generated to expose this practical failure mode, and the forget targets are discovered in model outputs rather than planted through poisoning.
q1_evidence: Secs. 3.3 and 4.3 (PDF pp. 5, 7) identify hallucinated package tokens in model-generated responses through registry checks. Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 8) selects 20 initial coding prompts from a prior package-hallucination benchmark; Sec. 3.6 (PDF p. 6) mutates prompts to discover further failures. Appendix G (PDF pp. 16-17) fixes the PyPI snapshot across training and evaluation.
q2_assessment: The need for correction is directly established by initial-sampling failure screening and unmodified-model hallucination rates for both evaluated DeepSeek-Coder models. Because the prompts are deliberately difficult, these measurements characterize the selected stress setting rather than a representative deployment-wide failure rate.
q2_evidence: Sec. 4.4 (PDF p. 8) retains prompts whose initial base-model sampling includes both valid and hallucinated packages and explicitly notes the difficult selection. Secs. 4.5-4.6 (PDF pp. 8-9) define the unmodified baseline and registry-based hallucination rate; Table 1 (PDF p. 10) reports baseline rates of 21.23% for DeepSeek-7B and 27.75% for DeepSeek-16B.
q3_assessment: Registry-based rates support suppression of invalid package recommendations, and prompt-mutation experiments support generalization to unseen prompts within the studied Python setting. Registry validity does not establish semantic correctness of package use or execution of the target programs. EvalPlus execution tests separately assess retained general coding ability, while code/instruction KL measures non-target distribution drift; retention is model-dependent, with average utility improving for 7B but declining for 16B.
q3_evidence: Sec. 4.6 and Table 1 (PDF pp. 8-10) report hallucination rates falling to 2.56%/6.13% and HumanEval, HumanEval+, MBPP and MBPP+ Pass@1, whose averages change from 66.98% to 68.57% for 7B and from 77.4% to 73.17% for 16B. The same table separates code, instruction and package KL. Sec. 3.6 (PDF p. 6) reports unseen-prompt evaluation after mutation, and Sec. 6.0.3/Fig. 7 (PDF p. 12) ablates mutation count. Sec. 7 (PDF p. 12) explicitly limits the oracle to name existence and the evaluation to Python and two DeepSeek models.
